prompt: A social feed shows an infinite-scrolling list of posts that are inserted constantly, and users only ever scroll forward from most recent. Which pagination approach fits best, and why?
choices: Offset-based, because LIMIT/OFFSET is simpler to implement
Cursor-based, because it's anchored to a specific row so new inserts don't shift a user's position or cause duplicates/skips
Offset-based, because it allows jumping directly to page 50
Neither is needed since the dataset is small

prompt: Why does idempotency matter specifically for POST requests but not usually for GET?
choices: POST requests are always slower than GET requests

GET is defined to be safe and idempotent by HTTP's own semantics, while POST creates a new resource each time by default, so a retried POST (e.g. after a lost response) can duplicate an action like a payment
GET requests cannot include a request body, so they never need protection
POST requests are never retried by clients

prompt: In an idempotency-key implementation, a client sends the same Idempotency-Key twice but with a different request body the second time. What should the server do?
choices: Silently process the second request as a new operation
Return the cached response from the first request without checking the body
Reject the request with an error, since reusing a key with a different payload signals a client-side bug
Merge the two request bodies before processing

prompt: What is the main advantage of a token bucket algorithm over a fixed-window rate limit (e.g. exactly 100 requests per calendar minute)?
choices: It never rejects any requests
It requires no server-side state
It allows short bursts up to the bucket capacity while still enforcing a steady average rate, avoiding the abrupt reset/dogpile behavior of a hard window boundary
It only works for authenticated clients

prompt: In an OpenAPI spec, what is the purpose of using $ref to point to a components/schemas definition like Order instead of inlining the same object structure in every response?
choices: It makes the API run faster at request time
It's required syntax with no functional benefit
It defines the shape once and reuses it everywhere referenced, preventing the schema from drifting out of sync across endpoints
It automatically adds authentication to the endpoint

prompt: A mobile app needs a lightweight order-list view (id, status, total) and a heavy order-detail view (order plus customer, address, and line items) from the same backend. Which statement best captures the realistic REST-vs-GraphQL trade-off here?
choices: GraphQL is always the wrong choice for mobile apps

REST requires either two separate endpoints or over-fetching on the list view, while a single GraphQL endpoint can request exactly the fields each screen needs in one round trip — this is a case where GraphQL's flexibility genuinely pays off
REST cannot support more than one endpoint per resource, so this isn't possible in REST at all
GraphQL eliminates the need for any server-side validation or rate limiting
